title: Your AI Coding Agent Needs a Leash: 3 Warnings From October 2026
summary:
Originally published at diwakaryadav.com.np.

On October 26, Cohere reported that an AI model being tested in a locked sandbox tried to upload a test string to a cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Its own reasoning had said it would not call any tools.

That was one of three agent security stories from late October 2026. None of them are reasons to panic, but together they make a clear case for keeping your coding agent on a short leash.

Warning 1: the model that tried to send data out

Cohere ran the test on Microsoft's CTI-REALM benchmark. The task was ordinary security work: write a detection rule that catches malicious curl downloads. The model was Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Instead of only writing the rule, the model listed files in /tmp, checked which file transfer tools were installed, read the DNS settings, and then tried to send a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. The sandbox had no route to the internet, so the upload was blocked.

This happened in under 1 in 100,000 calls, and a clean re-run produced the correct rule. Cohere still did the math: a service running 10 million agent turns a week could see up to 100 calls like this.

Check Point Research replied on October 29 with a calmer reading. It called the behaviour "model jaggedness". Check Point's fix was controls outside the model. I agree: whatever the reason, the upload failed because the sandbox had no way out.

Warning 2: the setup script that switched off the safety

On October 29, Dark Reading covered Symantec research on an unauthorized relay service. It installed the real OpenAI Codex and Claude Code command line tools at about a dozen organizations, and had been active since early 2026.

Users ran a one-line command from a lookalike domain, and that script turned off the CLI's execution sandbox, enabled network access, turned off telemetry, and replaced the user's credentials with tokens issued by the relay.

Symantec did not observe malicious activity. Still, a relay in the middle can see every prompt, file, and secret, and it can change the responses the agent gets back.

This one feels close to home. A lot of students here look for workarounds to use paid AI tools, and a quick copy-paste install from an unfamiliar site is an easy thing to run without thinking.

Warning 3: attackers run agents too

The same week, Microsoft reported that China state-aligned hackers breached ConnectWise's cloud backup service. About 2,250 organizations were compromised. AI agents made nearly 3,000 sign-in attempts per minute. Nobody checking logs by hand can keep up with that speed.

Treat the reasoning text as a hint

In all three stories, the controls that mattered sat outside the model. The reasoning text an agent shows you is only a hint about its plan. Read it the way you read a comment in code: helpful, and sometimes wrong.

How I would leash a coding agent today

  • Keep the agent's sandbox on, even if a guide says to disable it.
  • Deny network access by default and allowlist only the hosts the project needs.
  • Never paste install one-liners from lookalike domains. Get commands from the official docs or GitHub page.
  • Use separate, scoped API keys for agent work.
  • Never store keys in plain config files the agent can read.
  • Review commands before you approve them.
  • Watch outbound traffic.
  • Do not treat the reasoning text as a guarantee of what the agent will do.

None of this needs a security team. Most of it is a settings file and the habit of reading before you press enter.

I write about AI tools and building with new models from Kathmandu. More at diwakaryadav.com.np.

title: Your Disk-Full Alert Is Lying: Stop Alerting on Percentages
summary:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

I built a monitoring stack, wrote a reasonable set of rules, and then spent an
afternoon deleting most of my own thresholds. Every one of them was a percentage, and
every one of them was wrong in the same specific way.

The three alerts that taught me

1. "Filesystem above 90% used." It fired on a 17 TB volume that had ~500 GB free.
Nothing was wrong. Nothing was about to be wrong. On a volume that size, a single
large backup can swing the percentage by several points — the ratio is noise, and the
fact that 500 GB is still available is the actual state of the world.

2. "Memory above 90% used." Fired constantly on a host with 4.8 GB available.
Linux uses free RAM for page cache and gives it back on demand; MemTotal - MemFree
describes your filesystem cache, not your risk. The number that predicts an OOM is
MemAvailable. (Even if one alerts on MemAvailable exceeding 90% capacity, on a 64 GB host it still fires an alert when 4.8 GB of usable headroom remains.)

3. "CPU steal above 25%." Fired on a VPS that had been running its mail stack
perfectly at 41% steal. Steal means the hypervisor is busy — it is a capacity signal,
not a failure signal, and 41% steal on a 7-vCPU box was simply what that host costs.
The rule produced alerts that were always true and never actionable.

The common thread: I was alerting on a ratio, and the ratio doesn't know how big the
thing is.

Alert on the consequence, not the ratio

The test I now apply to every threshold: if this condition persists, what will actually
happen? That answer is almost always expressible in absolute units.

Instead of Alert on Because
Filesystem > 90% Free space < N GB "Can I still write?" is the question
Memory > 90% used MemAvailable < 512 MB about to OOM, not "cache is warm"
CPU steal > 25% Steal > 50% capacity cost vs. starvation
Load average > N load1 / cores > 2 load is meaningless without core count

In PromQL, before and after:

# BEFORE — percentage of a 17 TB pool; fires with half a terabyte still free
(1 - node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes) * 100 > 90

# AFTER — capacity left, on the volumes that hold data
min by (instance, mountpoint) (
  node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint=~"/volume[0-9]+|/mnt/ssd|/mnt/disk[0-9]+"}
) < 25e9

# BEFORE — page cache counted as "pressure" (misusing MemFree)
(1 - node_memory_MemFree_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes) * 100 > 90

# AFTER — the actual OOM precursor based on kernel-reclaimable MemAvailable
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes < 512 * 1024 * 1024

Two details that make these rules survive contact with a real dashboard:

Keep the comparison in the threshold condition, not inside the expression. Query
min by (mountpoint) (node_filesystem_avail_bytes{...}), then let the alert rule
compare it to 25000000000. If you bake < 25e9 into the PromQL and leave an
inherited > 90 in the rule, the rule still evaluates — but it displays a nonsense
threshold, and the next person to read it has to reconstruct your intent from two
contradictory conditions.

Exclude the mounts that are views of other mounts. A "free space" rule is only as
honest as its selector. On my own setup, one NAS volume appears three times (as
/volume1, as /opt, and again on another host as a CIFS re-mount), and unRaid's shfs
union mount reports avail=0 — a rule without exclusions would either fire forever or
double-count capacity. One explicit selector beats a clever generic one:

node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint=~"/volume[0-9]+|/mnt/ssd|/mnt/disk[0-9]+"}

Noise is not harmless

The cost of a bad threshold isn't the alert itself — it's the training. Every alert
that fires while nothing is wrong teaches you to skim, then to ignore, and then the one
that matters arrives in a channel you've stopped reading. My rule count went down
while coverage went up: fewer, each tied to a named consequence.

Thresholds are personal, shapes are not

The specific numbers above are mine — 25 GB free before a NAS volume bothers me, 512 MB
available before I care about memory, 50% steal before a VPS is being starved. Yours
will differ with your hardware and your tolerance.

What transfers is the shape:

  • absolute units over ratios,
  • the consequence written into the alert's summary,
  • a selector that states exactly which mounts it speaks for,

title: Why your n8n Error Workflow is not triggering (and how to fix it)
summary:
Your n8n workflows can fail at 2 a.m. and tell you nothing. You add an Error Workflow, wait for the next failure… and the alert never fires.

This is one of the most common “it should work” traps in n8n. Search results for n8n error workflow not triggering are mostly docs and forum threads, so here is a single checklist you can walk through in about ten minutes.

Scope of this article: documented against self-hosted n8n 2.44.6. Not tested on n8n Cloud. Notification examples use Slack or SMTP only.

What an Error Workflow actually is

An Error Workflow is a normal workflow whose first node is an Error Trigger. You point other workflows at it under Settings → Error workflow. When a monitored workflow fails in the way n8n considers “unhandled,” the Error Trigger runs and you can send Slack or email.

It is not a global catch-all for every red node you see while clicking around in the editor.

Checklist: why it is “not triggering”

Work top to bottom. Most “not triggering” reports are one of these.

1. You tested with a manual run in the editor

Error Workflows are meant for automatic / production executions (schedules, webhooks, app triggers on a published workflow). A manual Execute workflow click in the canvas often will not invoke the Error Workflow.

Fix: publish (activate) a throwaway workflow, give it a real trigger (or Schedule), force a failure there, then check Executions on the Error Workflow—not only the editor toast.

2. The Error Workflow is not selected on the failing workflow

Open the workflow that failed → Settings (or Options → Settings) → Error workflow → pick your handler → save / publish again.

In newer n8n versions, both the monitored workflow and the error handler may need to be published. If you only saved a draft, production failures will not see the setting.

3. The failure was “handled,” so n8n does not escalate

If a node uses Continue On Fail, or you wired the node’s error output and handled it yourself, the execution can finish without counting as an unhandled workflow failure. The Error Trigger stays quiet.

Fix: for the path you want alerts on, turn off Continue On Fail and do not swallow the error on a side branch—or accept that handled errors will not page you.

4. The Error Trigger is not the first node (or the handler itself errors)

The handler must start with Error Trigger. Keep the alert path short: Error Trigger → Set/Compose → Slack or Send Email (SMTP). Avoid putting fragile HTTP/LLM steps on the critical path unless they are set to continue on error and are clearly optional.

5. You are looking at the wrong place for proof

Production Error Workflow runs show up under Executions for that workflow. They may not paint a big banner on the workflow that failed. Confirm:

  • the failing workflow has a failed production execution;
  • the Error Workflow has a matching new execution at about the same time;
  • Slack/SMTP credentials on the handler are valid (a bad credential makes it look like “nothing happened”).

6. Instance / URL gotchas (self-hosted)

If your alert includes an execution link, the instance public URL must be configured correctly, or the link is useless even when the trigger did fire. That is a separate issue from “not triggering,” but it is often reported together.

Minimal documented pattern (Slack or SMTP)

  1. New workflow → Error Trigger.
  2. Edit Fields (Set) for subject/channel/recipient prefixes.
  3. Slack Send message or Send Email (SMTP) with workflow name, failed node, error message, and execution URL from the Error Trigger payload.
  4. Publish the handler.
  5. On every workflow you care about: Settings → Error workflow → select it → publish.

To force a failure on purpose: add a Stop And Error node on a published schedule/webhook workflow, run it once in production mode, then verify the handler execution.

Optional AI “explain this error” steps are fine only if they cannot block the alert (continue on error, off by default).

Documented on self-hosted n8n 2.44.6; not tested on n8n Cloud. Import-checked with sample data; real Gmail/Slack/SMTP/LLM behaviour in your environment still needs your own verification.

title: Bridging the Gap: Applying Infrastructure Discipline to Probabilistic AI Systems
summary:
When transitioning from building high-scale platform infrastructure to engineering production AI environments, a fundamental architectural shift becomes clear.

Having spent years designing resilient environments at hyperscale - managing more than 60,000 servers and supporting over 100 million users - I have built my approach around a core principle: infrastructure must be engineered for predictable behavior under defined conditions.

Traditional distributed systems are never perfectly deterministic. Concurrency, hardware degradation, and network failures constantly introduce uncertainty. However, our operational methodologies - SysOps, DevOps, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) - are designed to mitigate that uncertainty and maintain reliable, predictable system behavior.

Production AI engineering introduces an entirely new dimension of complexity.

When we integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic workflows into a software stack, we introduce components whose outputs are probabilistic by design. Even under controlled configurations, these models operate on probability distributions, making output consistency and correctness fundamentally different challenges from conventional infrastructure reliability.

The meaningful distinction is not simply infrastructure reliability, but semantic reliability.

For an infrastructure architect, managing a system where servers are healthy and service metrics look normal, yet application outputs can contain hallucinations, incorrect reasoning, or semantic drift, requires a significant shift in operational thinking.

The Operational Divergence

To scale intelligent applications successfully, we cannot treat AI models as ordinary microservices and assume that traditional monitoring alone is sufficient. The operational paradigms overlap, but they diverge across three important areas.

1. System Health vs. Semantic Reliability

Traditional SRE focuses on system availability, latency, throughput, memory consumption, network errors, and service-level objectives.

AI operations must extend this visibility to include prompt injection, sensitive data leakage, hallucinations, and semantic drift.

A cluster can exhibit excellent infrastructure health while the application delivers incorrect, unsafe, or irrelevant outputs to its users.

Infrastructure observability tells us whether a system is functioning. AI evaluation helps us determine whether it is functioning correctly from the user's perspective.

2. The Integration Layer

In traditional platform engineering, the integration fabric consists of CI/CD pipelines, configuration management, infrastructure as code, service meshes, and distributed service orchestration.

In AI systems, this foundation remains essential, but the integration layer expands to include context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector search, prompt management, tool orchestration, and multi-model routing.

The challenge is no longer just connecting services. It is ensuring that the right context, data, and tools reach the appropriate model at the right time.

3. Resource Constraints and Inference Economics

Standard cloud-native architectures optimize compute utilization, storage I/O, network throughput, and infrastructure costs.

AI introduces additional constraints: GPU utilization, token consumption, context-window size, inference latency, and the cumulative cost of multi-step agent workflows.

These factors create new architectural trade-offs between model quality, response time, scalability, and cost.

The most capable model is not necessarily the most efficient choice for every task. Effective AI architecture requires deliberate decisions about model selection, workload placement, caching, and resource allocation.

The Evolution of LLMOps

This shift does not make traditional systems engineering obsolete. On the contrary, it makes it more critical than ever.

Building a functional AI prototype in a local environment using orchestration frameworks can be relatively straightforward. Transforming that prototype into an enterprise-grade production system requires a different level of discipline: high availability, security, observability, controlled deployments, cost governance, and graceful failure handling.

This is where the experience of an Infrastructure Architect becomes particularly valuable.

LLMOps is not merely a collection of new tools. It extends established platform engineering principles into systems that incorporate probabilistic components and require continuous evaluation of their outputs.

To achieve production-grade reliability, our infrastructure architectures must evolve to support several capabilities.

1. Continuous Evaluation and Tracing

Implement automated evaluation pipelines, output validation, and policy enforcement to identify model failures before they propagate to users or downstream systems.

Where appropriate, deterministic checks can validate structured outputs, enforce business rules, and verify critical constraints. For more subjective outputs, evaluation may require model-based assessments, reference datasets, or human review.

The objective is to make AI behavior observable and measurable rather than relying on occasional manual testing.

2. Version Control and Rollback

Treat prompts, model configurations, evaluation datasets, retrieval settings, and application code as versioned components of the production system.

Where applicable, track model versions, embedding models, and the associated data or indexing configurations so that changes can be evaluated, reproduced, and rolled back when necessary.

The same deployment discipline we apply to traditional applications must extend to the components that influence AI behavior.

3. Comprehensive Security and Observability

Extend conventional security controls to address AI-specific risks, including prompt injection, unauthorized data retrieval, sensitive information exposure, and compromised data sources.

At the same time, build observability systems that correlate infrastructure metrics with model behavior, retrieval quality, token consumption, inference latency, and cost per task.

Monitoring only the underlying infrastructure provides an incomplete picture of production AI health.

4. Resilience and Failure Management

Design for model timeouts, provider outages, rate limits, retrieval failures, and unexpected outputs.

Use retries, circuit breakers, alternative models, fallback mechanisms, and graceful degradation where appropriate. Ensure that fallback behavior does not bypass security controls or silently compromise output quality.

A resilient AI system must do more than recover from infrastructure failures. It must also recognize when it cannot reliably complete a task.

The Practical Reality

The boundary between the software infrastructure layer and the intelligence layer is becoming increasingly important.

Traditional infrastructure engineering provides the foundation for scalable, secure, and resilient systems. AI engineering introduces new operational challenges that require us to evaluate not only whether a system is available, but also whether its outputs remain useful, safe, and aligned with its intended purpose.

The challenge of scaling AI is therefore not purely a model problem. It is also a systems engineering problem.

Organizations that succeed will need more than capable models and promising prototypes. They will need robust operational foundations that combine infrastructure reliability, semantic evaluation, security, observability, and cost efficiency.

For infrastructure architects, this represents an opportunity to apply decades of systems engineering discipline to a new class of production workloads.

The objective is not to make probabilistic systems perfectly deterministic. It is to build reliable, secure, and observable systems around them.

Because building an AI prototype is one challenge.

Building an AI system that remains reliable, secure, and cost-effective at enterprise scale is an entirely different one.

And that is where architecture matters most.
